sources.text: Jämtland Triangle – hiking guide | Swedish Tourist Association Hike the Jämtland triangle The Jämtland triangle Jämtlandstriangeln is one of Sweden's most classic mountain hikes, and it suits both first-time mountain hikers and those with more experience. The trail runs between Storulvån, Sylarna and Blåhammaren through a varied and magnificent mountain landscape. Jämtlandstriangeln is usually hiked over three days: from Storulvån Mountain station to Sylarna Mountain station , on to Blåhammaren and back to Storulvån. Or in the opposite direction. Since the route takes you from one mountain station to the next, you don’t need to carry a tent or food for the entire hike. Each place has a shop and a self-catering kitchen, and Storulvån and Sylarna also have a restaurant. In Storulvån you can rent equipment such as skis and a backpack. Reindeer herding is practiced in this area, thank you for showing consideration! Learn more about how to avoid disturbing the reindeer. Navigate past video or other external content. För att titta på videon måste du godkänna marknadsföringscookies . Skipped past external content, go back. Jämtland triangle facts Total distance: 47 km Number of stages/days: 3 Stage length: 12–18 km (4–8 hours of hiking per day) Food & water: Shops and self-catering kitchens are available at all accommodations along the route. Breakfast and dinner are served at Storulvån and Sylarna mountain stations, which are fully licensed. For lunches and breaks, you’ll need to bring your own food and drinks. Water can be collected from streams. Accommodation along the route : STF Storulvån Mountain station , STF Sylarna Mountain station and STF Blåhammaren Map: The “Fjällkartan” app, Lantmäteriet map “Z54” or a Calazo map of the Jämtland Triangle Map of the Jämtland Triangle Navigate past map or other external content. This map is a planning tool and should not replace a physical map and compass. The service “Naturkartan” (opens in new tab) is operated by a company called “Outdoor map”. Please note that trail information is owned and updated by the respective trail administrator (e.g. municipality or county administrative board). Skipped past external content, go back. Book accommodation Jämtland triangle STF Storulvån Mountain station The Jämtland mountains Average guest rating 4.7 out of 5 4.7 Book accommodation STF Blåhammaren The Jämtland mountains Average guest rating 4.3 out of 5 4.3 Book accommodation STF Sylarna Mountain station The Jämtland mountains Average guest rating 4.7 out of 5 4.7 Book accommodation Show all accommodations Jämtland Triangle hiking packages Storulvån – Family mountain adventure on your own The Jämtland mountains On your own Multiple days From 2,676/1,312 SEK Show all activities Getting to the trail Take the train to Duved or Enafors. From there, you can book a transfer by bus or taxi to Storulvån via wansethbuss.se (opens in new tab). If you are driving, take the E14 towards Åre and turn off towards Duved. From the E14 in Enafors, there are signs to Storulvån. There is parking and the option to charge an electric car. Please note! Between 1 February and 15 April, the road between Handöl and Storulvån is closed at night, 22:00–08:00. The road may also close during the day in bad weather. The nearest airports are Östersund/Åre Airport and Trondheim/Værnes Airport. The Jämtland Triangle with a tent The Jämtland Triangle is also popular if you want to hike with a tent. The right of public access applies along most of the trail, but keep in mind that reindeer herding is practised throughout the area. If you want to camp near a mountain station, you pay a camping and service fee . This gives you access to the self-catering kitchen, sauna and toilets, making it possible to combine the freedom of a tent with the comforts of the stations. The fee is paid on site. Don’t miss Stay an extra day at Sylarna and climb Syltoppen—a high alpine and exciting experience. Stages of the Jämtland Triangle Tip! Sleep the first night at STF Storulvån Mountain Station Stage 1: Storulvån-Sylarna 16 kilometres, 5–7 hours of hiking Accommodation: STF Sylarna Mountain Station The first kilometres pass through mountain birch forest. After crossing the suspension bridge over Lill-Ulvån, the trail continues above the tree line all the way to the destination. The route climbs gently throughout, with only a few exceptions. The famous silhouette of the Sylarna peaks is visible for most of the day. After about eight kilometres, you reach the Spåjme shelter, a popular spot for a break if the weather is rough. Water can be collected from streams along the way. At the station, there is a self-catering kitchen as well as a fully licensed restaurant. Stage 2: Sylarna-Blåhammaren 19 kilometres, 6–8 hours of hiking Accommodation: STF Blåhammaren The day begins with a descent to the Enan river, followed by rolling terrain with both uphill and downhill sections. After the first climb, you’ll be rewarded with stunning views of the Sylarna massif—so don’t forget to look back! About halfway, you’ll reach the Enkälen shelter, a good spot for a break. The day ends with an uphill stretch. This stage takes you through varied and sometimes rocky terrain that can also be quite exposed to strong winds. Water can be collected from streams along the way. At the station, there is a self-catering kitchen and a shop where you can buy supplies. Around 4 km south of Blåhammaren, you may need to wade across a stream during periods of high water. Also keep in mind that reindeer herding takes place in the area, so be respectful and show consideration. Stage 3: Blåhammaren-Storulvån 12 kilometres, 4–5 hours of hiking Accommodation: STF Storulvån Mountain Station The final day can generally be described as flat, downhill, flat and downhill—an easy hike overall. After six kilometres, you’ll reach the Ulvåtjärn shelter. The surroundings here are almost magical, with steep sandy ridges and gently flowing streams. The trail then crosses a stream that needs to be forded. After the crossing, you walk across an ancient lakebed from the last Ice Age. The route ends as it began—in mountain birch forest. Water can be collected from streams along the way. At the station, there is a self-catering kitchen and a fully licensed restaurant. Trail markings Check the trail markings before you set out. Winter trails are marked with crosses, while summer trails are marked with painted poles, stones, or trees. Winter trails can be difficult to follow in summer, so use a map and trail signs to navigate. Read more about the trail system Visitor calendar Do you prefer a quieter experience in the mountains? Our visitor calendar gives you an overview of typical occupancy levels in this mountain area, helping you plan your trip during less busy periods. During quieter times, we also often offer better prices. Please note that the visitor calendar is only an indication and does not account for variations due to events or holidays.
